title: The belly and the bed: why opponents hate fasting
english: I would be surprised at these unspiritual Christians if they were held only by luxury, since they marry rather often, and not also ruled by gluttony, since they hate fasting. Lust without gluttony would surely be considered a monster, since these two are so united and fused together that if they could be separated at all, the private parts would not be the first to cling to the belly. Look at the body: it is one region. In fact, the order of vices follows the arrangement of the members. The belly comes first, and immediately the rest of lust is built upon overindulgence; through greediness, lust passes over. I recognize, then, an unspiritual faith by its devotion to the flesh, of which it entirely consists, as prone to much eating as to much marrying, so that it rightly accuses spiritual discipline as hostile to its substance in this kind of self-control as well, since that discipline puts reins on gluttony through food that is sometimes none, sometimes late, sometimes dry, just as it does on lust through single marriages.

It is now tiresome to engage with such people; it is even shameful to dispute about them, since their defense is not even respectable. How am I to protect chastity and sobriety without censuring my opponents? Who they are I will name once: the outer and inner gluttons among the unspiritual Christians. These people make controversy against the Advocate, the Holy Spirit; for this reason the New Prophecy is rejected—not because Montanus and Priscilla and Maximilla preach another God, nor because they dissolve Jesus Christ, nor because they overturn any rule of faith or hope, but because they plainly teach fasting more often than marrying. About the manner of marrying, I have already published a defense of monogamy. Now the battle over the discipline of food is the second, or rather the first, fight for self-control.

They accuse us because we keep our own fasts, because we often extend station fasts until evening, because we also observe dry-food fasts, keeping our food free of all meat and all juiciness and any of the more succulent fruits, and we neither eat nor drink anything with a winey quality; we also abstain from bathing, which suits dry-food fasts. So they object to novelty, and from its unlawfulness they prescribe that it must be judged heresy if it is human presumption, or pronounced false prophecy if it is a spiritual command, so that on every side we hear anathema, we who proclaim otherwise.
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by attacking the unspiritual Christians who oppose the New Prophecy's fasting practices, tracing their hostility to gluttony and lust.

title: Opponents' objections from Scripture and custom
english: Now as for fasting, they set against us certain days appointed by God. In Leviticus the Lord commands Moses that the tenth day of the seventh month is a day of atonement: "It shall be a holy day for you, and you shall afflict your souls, and every soul that is not afflicted on that day shall be cut off from his people" (Leviticus 16:29). In the gospel they think the days of fasting are fixed as those in which the bridegroom was taken away (Matthew 9:15), and that these are now the only lawful fasts for Christians, since the legal and prophetic old things have been abolished. For where it suits them, they recognize what 'the law and the prophets until John' means (Matthew 11:13). And so from then on one must fast without distinction, by choice, not by the command of a new discipline, according to each person's times and causes. They say the apostles observed this too, imposing no other yoke of fixed fasts to be kept by all in common, and likewise no station fasts—which indeed have their own days, the fourth feria and the sixth, but run without distinction, neither under the law of a command nor beyond the end of the day, since prayers generally conclude at the ninth hour, from Peter's example reported in the Acts (Acts 3:1).

Dry-food fasts, however, they call a new name for an affected practice, and next door to pagan superstition—the sort of chastities that purify Apis, Isis, and the Great Mother by excluding certain foods. For faith in Christ is free, and does not owe even the Jewish law abstinence from certain foods, since the whole meat market was once for all admitted by the apostle, who detested those who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods created by God (1 Timothy 4:3). And so they say we were already marked out then, in the last times, departing from the faith, attending to seducing spirits of the world, having a conscience seared by the doctrines of liars (1 Timothy 4:1-2). Branded by what fires, I ask you? By the fires, I suppose, with which we often conduct weddings and cook dinners every day? So too they say that with the Galatians we are struck down as observers of days and months and years (Galatians 4:10).

Meanwhile they hurl at us that Isaiah declared: "The Lord has not chosen such a fast" (Isaiah 58:5)—that is, not abstinence from food, but the works of justice which he goes on to list. And that the Lord himself in the gospel answered every scrupulosity about food with a summary: a man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of his mouth (Matthew 15:11), since he himself ate and drank to the point of being marked: "Behold, a glutton and a drinker!" (Matthew 11:19). So too the apostle teaches that food does not commend us to God: we are no better if we eat, nor worse if we do not eat (1 Corinthians 8:8).

With these and similar arguments they now press so subtly that anyone more inclined to his belly can consider the duties of removing, reducing, or postponing food as superfluous and not really necessary—God, of course, preferring works of justice and innocence. And we know what the persuasions of fleshly comforts are like, how easily it is said: "What I need is to believe with my whole heart, to love God and my neighbor as myself. For on these two commands hang the whole law and the prophets" (Matthew 22:37-40)—not on the emptiness of my lungs and intestines.
orientation: Tertullian is reporting the objections of the unspiritual Christians against the New Prophecy's fasting practices, quoting their appeals to Scripture and apostolic custom.

title: The original sin of eating and fasting as its remedy
english: So I must first defend what is being quietly undermined: how much this emptiness is worth before God, and above all, where the very logic of earning God's favor in this way came from. For the necessity of the observance will be recognized once the authority of its rationale shines out, and that rationale must be traced from the beginning.

Adam had received from God the law not to taste of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and he would die if he tasted it. But after his spiritual ecstasy, in which he had prophesied that great mystery of Christ and the church, he fell back into a merely unspiritual state. No longer able to grasp the things of the Spirit, he yielded to his belly more easily than to God, nodded to food rather than to the command, and sold his salvation for gluttony. He ate, and he perished, though he would have been safe if he had chosen to fast from one little tree. From this point on, let unspiritual faith recognize its own seed, deriving from there its appetite for fleshly things and its rejection of spiritual things.

I hold, then, that from the very beginning gluttony is a murderer, to be punished with the torments and penalties of hunger, even if God had commanded no fasts. Yet by showing me where Adam was slain, God left me to understand the remedies for the offense, since he had shown me the offense itself. Of my own accord I would count food as poison, in whatever ways and at whatever times I could, and take hunger as an antidote, through which I might purge the cause of death that had been passed down from the beginning into me along with the race itself. I would be certain that God wills this, whose contrary he did not will, and confident enough that the discipline of self-control would please him, since I had learned that the fault of lack of self-control was condemned by him.

Furthermore, since he himself commands fasting and calls a crushed soul, crushed precisely by the straits of food, a sacrifice, who will now doubt that this was the rationale of all mortifications of appetite: that by again forbidding food and observing the command, the original sin might be expiated, so that through the same material of the cause, the prohibition of food, man might make satisfaction to God through the very thing by which he had offended, and so fasting might rekindle salvation, just as overindulgence had extinguished it, by despising many permitted foods in place of the one forbidden one?
orientation: Tertullian is answering the opponents' claim that fasting is unnecessary by going back to God's first command to Adam in Eden.

title: Why God did not impose fasting at first
english: This was the plan God's providence followed, arranging all things according to their times, so that no one could turn it against us and say: Why then did God not immediately impose some chastisement of food, and instead even increased the permission? For in the beginning he assigned man only grassy and tree food: "See, I have given you every seed-bearing plant that sows seed, which is upon the earth, and every tree that has in itself the fruit of seed that sows seed—it will be food for you" (Genesis 1:29). But later, to Noah, after listing the subjection of all the beasts of the earth, the birds of the sky, the creatures that move on the earth, the fish of the sea, and every serpent, he said: "They will be food for you; like the green plants I have given you all things. But you shall not eat flesh in the blood of its life" (Genesis 9:2-4). For by this very fact—that he exempts from eating only that flesh whose life is not poured out through the blood—it is clear that he granted the use of all other flesh.

To this we answer that it was not fitting for man to be burdened with any law of self-control who was at that very time unable to endure so light a prohibition—that of a single fruit. Therefore he was to be strengthened by freedom itself, having been released. Likewise after the flood, in the renewal of the human race, one law for the time being was enough: to abstain from blood, while the use of everything else was permitted. For the Lord had already shown his judgment through the flood, and he had also threatened the requiring of blood from the hand of a brother and from the hand of every beast (Genesis 9:5). So, administering the justice of judgment beforehand, he sent out the material of freedom, preparing discipline through pardon—permitting all things so that he might take some away, intending to demand more if man committed more, intending to command self-control after he had first granted indulgence. In this way, as we have said, the original sin might be expiated by the working of a greater self-control in the occasion of a greater license.
orientation: Tertullian is answering an objection: if fasting is God's original discipline, why did God not command it from the beginning but instead first gave herbs and later all animals as food?

title: Israel's food discipline and the belly's complaint
english: Then, when a people already belonging to God began to be chosen and the restoration of man could be renewed, all the laws and disciplines were imposed, including those that would cut back food, with certain things removed as unclean, so that man might more easily endure fasting at times, having become accustomed to permanent abstinence from some foods. For the first people had re-engraved the crime of the first man, caught as more inclined to the belly than to God. When he was rescued from the harshness of Egyptian slavery by the mighty hand of God and the uplifted arm, and his Lord was seen, destined for a land flowing with milk and honey, he was immediately scandalized by the sight of the barren wilderness. Sighing over the loss of Egyptian fullness, he muttered against Moses and Aaron: "If only we had died struck down by the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat over pots of meat and ate bread to the full. Why have you led us out into this desert to kill this whole assembly with hunger?" (Exodus 16:3). He was going to lament the same leaders and arbiters of God with the same preference for the belly, whom he exasperated with his craving for meat and his recollection of Egyptian abundance. "Who will feed us meat? We remember the fish we ate in Egypt for free, and the cucumbers and melons and leeks and onions and garlic. But now our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing but manna" (Numbers 11:4-6). So even for them the angelic bread of manna was displeasing; they preferred the fragrance of garlic and onion to heaven. And therefore, from such ungrateful people, the more pleasing and delicious foods were taken away, both to punish gluttony and to train self-control, so that the one might be condemned and the other instructed.
orientation: Tertullian is showing that God imposed food restrictions on Israel so that, practiced in abstinence, they could more easily endure fasting, but the people preferred their bellies to God.

title: Fullness dulls the mind; fasting makes man equal to God
english: Now if we have rashly traced the reasons for a diet disciplined by God, and for one to be disciplined for God's sake, back to the experiments of the first beginnings, let us consult our common experience. Nature herself will declare what sort of people we used to be before food and drink, before any food or drink had touched our lips, in matters at least that are carried out by the sense through which divine things are handled: whether we were of much stronger mind, of much livelier heart, than when that whole dwelling of the inner man is stuffed with foods, flooded with wines, and already boiling to cook excrement, becoming preoccupied with the business of excretion, in which plainly nothing remains so close at hand as to have a taste for lust. "The people ate and drank, and they rose up to play" (Exodus 32:6). Understand the modesty of holy Scripture: it would not have marked the play unless it was shameless. But how few remember their religion when the places of memory are occupied, when the limbs of wisdom are hindered? No one will remember God as is fitting, as is right, as is useful, at that time when it is customary for the man himself to slip away from himself. Feeding either kills or wounds every discipline. I lie, if the Lord himself, reproaching Israel with forgetfulness of him, does not reckon the cause to fullness. "The beloved was fattened and made fat and enlarged, and he abandoned God who made him, and he departed from the Lord his savior" (Deuteronomy 32:15). Finally, in the same Deuteronomy, commanding that the same cause be guarded against, he says, "Lest, when you have eaten and drunk and built excellent houses, and your sheep and oxen have multiplied, and your heart be lifted up with silver and gold and you forget the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 8:12-14). He placed the enormity of voracity before the corruption of riches, which the riches themselves procure. Through it, of course, the heart of the people had been fattened, so that it could not see with eyes or hear with ears or perceive with heart, blocked by the fats which he specifically removed from eating, teaching man not to pursue overindulgence. But the one whose heart was found lifted up rather than fattened, who for forty days and as many nights made a fast last beyond the capacity of human nature, with spiritual faith supplying the strength, both saw with his eyes the glory of God and heard with his ears the voice of God and perceived with his heart the law of God, who even then was teaching that man does not live by bread alone but by every word of God (Deuteronomy 8:3) — although indeed the fatter people could not steadily contemplate even Moses himself, Moses, fed by God, his fasting fattened by God's name. Deservedly therefore the Lord also showed himself in the flesh to him, the colleague of his fasts, and no less to Elijah. For Elijah too had first consecrated himself sufficiently by fasts when he had called down famine. "The Lord lives," he says, "before whom I stand in his presence, if there will be dew in these years or rain." Then, fleeing the threatening Jezebel, after a single food and drink which he had found when awakened by an angel, he too arrived at Mount Horeb after forty days and nights with empty stomach and dry mouth, where, when he had turned aside into a cave, with what familiar meeting with God he was received! "What are you doing here, Elijah?" (1 Kings 19:9). How much friendlier is this voice than "Adam, where are you?" (Genesis 3:9). For that one threatened a man who had eaten; this one coaxed a man who was fasting. So great is the prerogative of a restricted diet, that it makes God a tent-companion to man, equal in truth to his equal. For if the eternal God will not hunger, as he testifies through Isaiah, this will be the time when man is made equal to God, when he lives without food.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that overindulgence in food and drink destroys memory of God and leads to sin, while fasting sharpens the mind and brings one near to God, as shown by Moses and Elijah.

title: Fasting as remedy: examples from Israel's history
english: We have now reached the examples, so let us review the effective powers of this duty's usefulness, which also reconciles an angry God to man. Israel had sinned at the watering place, gathered at Mizpah by Samuel, but so immediately washed away the sin by fasting that the danger of battle fled at the same time. While Samuel was offering the burnt offering—we hear of God's mercy being secured in nothing more than in the people's self-control—and the Philistines were moving into battle, the Lord thundered with a great voice over the Philistines, and they were thrown into confusion and fell before Israel, and the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines and struck them down as far as Beth-horon: the hungry cutting down the well-fed, the unarmed the armed. These will be the strengths of those who fast for God. Heaven fights for such people. You have the form of protection necessary even for spiritual wars.

Likewise, when Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, after many cities had already been captured, was directing blasphemies and threats against Israel through Rabshakeh, nothing else diverted him from his purpose toward Ethiopia. Then what else consumed 184,000 of his army through an angel but King Hezekiah's self-humbling? For when the enemy's harshness was announced, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and in the same dress ordered the elders of the priests to approach God through Isaiah, with fasting certainly accompanying the prayers. For there is no time for food in danger, nor is overindulgence the dress of sackcloth. Fasting is always the companion of grief, just as joy is the addition of overindulgence.

Through this companion of grief and fasting, that sinful city Nineveh was also freed from the destruction that had been proclaimed. For repentance had sufficiently commended the fasting of three days, even with the animals made to fast, with whom God was not angry. Sodom and Gomorrah would also have escaped if they had fasted.

Ahab also recognizes this remedy. When Elijah had reproached him after the transgression and idolatry and the murder of Naboth—killed by Jezebel for the vineyard—saying, 'How you have killed and taken possession! In the place where dogs licked Naboth's blood, they will also lick yours,' he set himself aside and put sackcloth on his flesh and fasted and slept in sackcloth. And then the word of the Lord came to Elijah: 'Have you seen how Ahab has shown reverence before my face? Because he has shown reverence, I will not bring disaster in his days, but in his son's days I will bring it'—the son who was not going to fast. So fasting is a work of reverence toward God, through which Hannah also, the wife of Elkanah, previously barren, easily obtained from God to fill her womb empty of food with a son, and indeed a prophet.

But not only changes of nature or the averting of dangers or the blotting out of sins, but also the recognition of sacred mysteries will fasts merit from God. Look at Daniel's example. Concerning the dream of the king of Babylon, all the wise men were troubled; they said it could no longer be known by human excellence. Daniel alone, trusting in God and knowing what to do to earn God's grace, asks for a space of three days, fasts with his companions, and so, with prayers commended, is instructed in the order and meaning of the dream in every detail. The tyrant's wise men are spared, God is glorified, Daniel is honored—and he was going to receive no less grace from God afterward, in the first year of King Darius, when from reconsidering the times proclaimed by Jeremiah he set his face toward God in fasts and sackcloth and ashes. For the angel sent to him immediately declared this as the cause of the divine favor: 'I have come,' he said, 'to show you, since you are pitiable'—by fasting, of course. If he was pitiable to God, he had been terrifying to the lions in the den, where indeed an angel procured a meal for him after six days of fasting.
orientation: Tertullian is now marshaling Old Testament examples to show that fasting reconciles an angry God to man, beginning with Israel at Mizpah under Samuel.

title: Christ and the apostles confirm fasting
english: We have given back the rest as well. But now we hurry on to new proofs. On the threshold of the Gospel stands Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel. She recognized the infant Lord and proclaimed many things about him to those awaiting the redemption of Israel. After the distinguished title of her long-standing and once-married widowhood, she is further honored by the testimony of her fasts. She shows in what duties one should attend to the church, and that Christ is understood by no one more than by those married once and often fasting.

Soon afterward the Lord himself dedicated his baptism, and in his own baptism that of all, with fasts. He had the power to make bread from stones, and perhaps even to make the Jordan flow with wine, if he had been such a glutton and drinker. Rather, he was initiating the new man, in reproach of the old man, by the power of despising food, so that he might show himself stronger through hunger to the devil, who was seeking to tempt him again through food. From then on he established the law that fasts must be carried out without sadness. For why should what is salutary be sad?

He also taught that battle must be waged against the more savage demons by fasts. For what wonder is it if an unclean spirit is driven out by the same operation by which the Holy Spirit is brought in? Finally, we read that the fasts of the centurion Cornelius, not yet baptized, were heard, just as the gracious regard of the Holy Spirit had hastened to him with the gift of prophecy besides. And I think the apostle, in the second letter to the Corinthians, among his labors and dangers and hardships, after hunger and thirst, also lists many fasts.
orientation: Tertullian is continuing his survey of biblical witnesses to fasting, now moving from Daniel to the New Testament examples of Anna, Christ, Cornelius, and Paul.

title: Dry-food fasts are ancient and effective
english: This primary form of discipline in food can already establish a precedent for the lesser practices of abstinence, showing that they too are useful or necessary in their own measure. For excluding certain foods is a partial fast. Let us then examine the novelty or emptiness of dry-food fasts, and see whether here too we are not dealing with a practice of religion that is as ancient as it is effective. I return to Daniel and his brothers, who preferred a diet of vegetables and water to the royal dishes and wine jars, and who became more handsome as a result—so that no one need fear for the body's appearance. Moreover, they were adorned in spirit. For God gave the young men knowledge and understanding in all literature, and to Daniel in every word, in dreams, and in all wisdom, so that he might also understand this very thing: the ways in which knowledge of the mysteries is obtained from God. Finally, in the third year of Cyrus king of the Persians, when he had fallen into reflection on a vision, he looked upon another form of self-humbling. "In those days," he says, "I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks. I did not eat pleasant bread, meat and wine did not enter my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil, until the three weeks were completed" (Daniel 10:2-3). When they were over, an angel was sent to him, speaking thus: "Daniel, you are a man to be pitied; do not be afraid, for from the first day when you gave your soul to reflection and self-humbling before God, your word was heard, and I have come because of your word" (Daniel 10:12). So the mercy of dry-food fasts and self-humbling drives out fear, turns God's ears toward us, and makes us possessors of hidden things. I return also to Elijah. Since ravens had been accustomed to fill him with bread and meat, why did a certain angel later offer him only bread and water when he was awakened from sleep near Beersheba in Judea? Had the ravens failed, which had fed him more generously? Or was it difficult for the angel to snatch some servant from a king's banquet with a fully loaded dish and carry him to Elijah, just as a meal from the reapers was presented to Daniel when he was hungry in the lions' den? But an example had to be established, teaching that in a time of pressure and persecution and any circumstance whatsoever, one must live on dry-food fasts. With such a diet David expressed his penitential confession, eating ashes as if they were bread—that is, bread as dry and filthy as ashes—and mixing his drink with weeping instead of wine. For abstinence from wine also has its own honors, which had consecrated Samuel to God and Aaron as well. For concerning Samuel, his mother says, "He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink" (1 Samuel 1:11); for she herself was praying to God in the same manner. And the Lord said to Aaron: "You and your sons after you shall not drink wine or strong drink whenever you enter the tabernacle or ascend to the altar, and you shall not die" (Leviticus 10:9). So those who minister in the church without sobriety will die. Thus he also reproaches Israel for the drink they gave: "You gave wine to my consecrated ones" (Amos 2:12). And this restriction of drink is a portion of the dry-food fast. Moreover, wherever abstinence from wine is either demanded by God or vowed by a person, there a restriction of food should also be understood, setting the pattern for the drink. For as the eating is, so is the drinking. It is not likely that anyone would offer half his gluttony to God—sober in water but drunk in food. And whether the apostle also knew dry-food fasts—he who had celebrated greater things, thirst and hunger and many fasts, who had refused drunkenness and reveling—is sufficiently argued from his disciple Timothy, whom he advised to use a little wine for his stomach and frequent illnesses (1 Timothy 5:23). Timothy abstained from wine not by rule but by devotion—for otherwise habit would have benefited his stomach more—and by this very advice Paul commended abstinence from wine as worthy of God, which he discouraged only out of necessity.
orientation: Tertullian is defending the New Prophecy's fasting practices, and has just argued that the chief form of fasting in food discipline can also establish the value of lesser abstinence practices.

title: Defending the late hour of station fasts
english: They likewise accuse our station fasts as commanded—and some of them set until late—under the name of novelty, saying that this duty too should be performed by personal choice and is not to be prolonged beyond the ninth hour, following their own custom, of course. But as far as the question of commanding goes, I will answer once for all cases. Now to the specific point of this particular practice—I mean the question of time—I must first take issue with them about the source from which they prescribe this rule of ending station fasts at the ninth hour. If it is because Peter and those with him are recorded as entering the temple at the ninth hour of prayer, who will prove to me that they were performing a station fast that day, so as to interpret the ninth hour as the close and discharge of the station? Yet you could more easily find that Peter, before taking food, first went up to the upper room at the sixth hour to pray, which would make the sixth hour the end of this duty, since it would seem to have been completed after prayer. Furthermore, since in the same commentary of Luke the third hour of prayer is also indicated—at which those filled with the Holy Spirit were considered drunk—and the sixth, at which Peter went up to the upper room, and the ninth, at which they entered the temple, why should we not understand that, while the freedom to pray always and everywhere and at every time remains entirely intact, those three hours were nonetheless more distinguished in human affairs—they divide the day, they mark off business, they resound publicly—and so were also more solemn in divine prayers? This is also suggested by the example of Daniel praying three times a day, certainly through the selection of certain hours, and no others than the more distinguished ones—the apostolic hours from then on: the third, the sixth, the ninth. From this, then, I would say that Peter observed the ninth hour from older custom, praying the third time as the final prayer of the day. But I say this for the sake of those who think they are acting from Peter's example, which they do not understand—not as though we reject the ninth hour, which we observe most fully on the fourth and sixth days of the week, but because for things observed from tradition we ought to give a more worthy reason to the extent that they lack scriptural authority, until they are either confirmed or corrected by some heavenly gift. And if you are ignorant of anything, he says, the Lord will reveal it to you. Therefore, setting aside the confirmer of all these things, the Advocate, the guide of all truth, ask whether a more worthy reason can be given among us for observing the ninth hour, so that this reason may also be assigned to Peter, if he was performing a station fast then. For it comes from the Lord's departure, which, although it ought always to be commemorated without distinction of hours, we are nevertheless more deeply bound to at that hour according to the very name of station. For soldiers too, never forgetful of their oath, obey station duty all the more. Therefore the fast itself is to be observed up to that hour in which, from the sixth hour, the darkened world mourned at the Lord's death, so that we too may return to joy when the world received back its light. If this savors more of Christian religion, while it celebrates Christ's glory more, I can equally fix the status of a late station from the same order of events, so that we fast until late, awaiting the time of the Lord's burial, when Joseph took away the body he had requested and laid it to rest. From this it is also irreligious for the flesh of servants to be refreshed before the Lord's. But let me have done with pressing conjectures against conjectures from the challenge of arguments—and yet, I think, striking back with more faithful ones. Let us see whether anything of this kind from ancient times also supports us. In Exodus, was not that posture of Moses fighting against Amalek with prayers, persisting until sunset, a late station fast? Do we think that Joshua, when he was defeating the Amorites, ate lunch on that day when he commanded a station for the very elements? The sun stood still in Gibeon and the moon in Aijalon; the sun and moon stood still until the people avenged themselves on their enemies, and the sun stood in mid-heaven (Joshua 10:12-13). But as it was moving toward its setting and the end of one day—there was no day like it before or after—it was so prolonged, he says, that God heard a man, as though the sun were his equal, pressing on so long in duty, a station even longer by being late. Certainly Saul too, when he was set in battle, openly commanded this duty: Cursed is the man who eats bread until evening, until I am avenged on my enemy—and none of his people tasted food, and the whole land was eating (1 Samuel 14:24). And God gave such authority to the edict of that station that Jonathan, Saul's son, although ignorant of the fast defined until late, had tasted a bit of honey, and was perhaps soon brought to trial for the offense and barely rescued from danger by the people's prayer. For he had been guilty of gluttony, though an unwitting one. But Daniel too, in the first year of King Darius, when he was fasting in sackcloth and ashes and making penitential confession to God, says: While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man whom I had seen in dreams at the beginning, flying swiftly, approached me about the hour of the evening sacrifice (Daniel 9:21). This will be the late station which, fasting until evening, offers a richer prayer to God.
orientation: Tertullian is answering opponents who accuse his group's station fasts of being a novelty because they extend them until evening, and he now argues from Scripture and tradition that the ninth hour and even later are fitting for ending a station.

title: The opponents' objection and the defense of the observances' authority
english: But I believe all these things are unknown to those who are disturbed by our practices. Or perhaps they have learned them only by reading, not by understanding, according to the greater influence of the inexperienced among that most glorious crowd, the unspiritual Christians. For this reason I have gone through each kind of observance: fasts, dry-food fasts, and station fasts. My purpose is this: while I review how much the duties of food, refused, cut back, or delayed, accomplish according to the arrangement of both testaments, I may blunt those who weaken these practices as if they were empty. At the same time, by showing that they have always held a place in true religion, I may refute those who accuse them of being new. For what has always existed is not new, and what is useful is not empty.

But there is also this point in the middle: some of these observances were commanded by God to humanity and so became law, while others were offered by humanity to God and so discharged a vow. Yet even a vow, when it has been accepted by God, becomes law for the future through the authority of the one who accepted it. For from that point on, the one who approved the deed commanded that it be done.

And so here another objection from the opposing side is brought forward in a different form. They say: either it is false prophecy, if a spiritual voice established these solemn observances, or it is heresy, if human presumption invented them. For they criticize the very pattern by which the old practices also came down to us, and by twisting this argument they could use it against the old practices as well, the same arguments that adversaries of the old ways could raise against them. So either they must reject those old practices too, or they must openly accept these new ones. This is especially necessary since these practices, from whatever founder they come, whether spiritual or merely faithful, run toward the same God as the old ones did. For without doubt both heresy and false prophecy will be judged by us, all of us priests of the one God the Creator and of his Christ, by their divergence from the divine nature. And so I defend this side without distinction, offering them whatever ground they wish to plant their foot on.

You say, O unspiritual Christian, that it is the spirit of the devil. And how does it prescribe duties belonging to our God, duties not to be offered to anyone but our God? Either argue that the devil works with our God, or let Satan be considered the Advocate. But you assert that he is a human antichrist, for this is the name heretics are called by in John. And how is it that whoever he is, he arranged these duties toward our Lord in our Christ, when antichrists have proceeded toward God but against our Christ? By what flanks, then, do you think the Spirit is confirmed among us, when he commands, or when he approves, the things that our God has both always commanded and always approved?

But again you fix boundary posts for God: for grace, so also for discipline; for spiritual gifts, so also for solemn observances, so that his duties have ceased just as his benefits have, and so you deny that he still imposes obligations, because here too the law and the prophets were until John. It remains for you to take away everything, as far as it lies in you, so idle.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the unspiritual Christians who object that the fasts, dry-food fasts, and station fasts are either false prophecy or heresy, and he is showing that these practices belong to the same God as the old observances.

title: The belly's reign and the martyr's discipline
english: For now, enriched and sated, you reign even in this kind of thing. You do not run against sins that fasting eliminates, nor do you need the knowledge of revelations that dry-food fasts extort, nor do you fear your own wars that station fasts scatter. So the Advocate would have fallen silent after John, and we ourselves would have become prophets for this very purpose—I no longer say to appease God's wrath or to obtain his protection or grace, but to fortify in advance through our own efforts the condition of the last times by proclaiming every form of self-control. Prison must be learned, hunger and thirst must be practiced, and endurance of both fasting and anxious diet must be made our own, so that a Christian enters prison the same kind of person he will come out—not about to suffer punishment there, but discipline; not the torments of the world, but his own duties. And he will go out to the contest all the more confident, having used his custody well, possessing nothing of the flesh, so that torments have no material to work on, since he is armored with skin alone, dry and horny against the claws, having already drained the blood that weighs down the soul, and the soul itself now hurrying on, since by frequent fasting it has already learned death from close at hand.

Clearly it is your way to provide cook-shops in prisons for uncertain martyrs, so they do not seek out the old habit, so they do not grow tired of life, so they are not scandalized by the new discipline of self-control. Not even your Pristinus, a non-Christian martyr, had touched that discipline. You had stuffed him for some time thanks to the freedom of his open custody, with all the baths as if better than baptism, all the retreats of luxury as if more secluded than the church, all the enticements of this life as if more worthy than eternal things—bound by all this, I think, he wanted to die. Finally, on the very day of his trial, in broad daylight, you medicated him in advance with unmixed wine as if with an antidote, and so enervated him that, scratched by a few claws (for this is what drunkenness felt), he could not answer the governor who asked him what lord he confessed, and so, already wrung out from this, having only hiccups and belches, he departed in the very act of denial. Therefore those who preach the discipline of sobriety are false prophets; therefore those who observe it are heretics. So why do you hesitate to believe in the Advocate whom you deny in Montanus, but believe in Apicius?
orientation: Tertullian is attacking his opponents for being rich and full-fed, and contrasting their pampered martyr Pristinus with the fasting discipline that prepares a Christian for prison and torture.

title: Tradition, innovation, and the Spirit's authority for fasts
english: You prescribe that the solemn observances of this faith were established by the Scriptures or by the tradition of the elders, and that nothing further in the way of observance may be added, because innovation is unlawful. Stand on that ground if you can. For look, I meet you as people who fast beyond Passover, apart from those days on which the bridegroom was taken away, who insert the half-fasts of station days, and who sometimes live on bread and water, as each of you sees fit. In the end you answer that these things are to be done by choice, not by command. So you have moved from your ground by going beyond tradition, since you practice things that were not established. But what kind of reasoning is it, that you allow to your own choice what you do not grant to God's command? Will more be permitted to human will than to divine power? I remember that I am free with respect to the world, not with respect to God. It is mine to perform a duty to the Lord of my own accord; it is his to command it. I owe him not only obedience but also devotion; the one I render at his command, the other by my own choice. It is well, too, that bishops are accustomed to command fasts for the whole people—I do not mean for the business of collecting contributions, as is your way of making gain, but sometimes also from some cause of ecclesiastical concern. Therefore, Therefore, if even at a human edict you all practise humiliation together as one, how do you censure in us that very unity of fasts, dry-food fasts, and station fasts?, how do you mark in us the very unity of fasts, dry-food fasts, and station fasts? Unless perhaps we are at fault in the decrees of the senate and the commands of emperors directed against assemblies. The Holy Spirit, when he was proclaiming in whatever lands and through whomever he wished, out of foreknowledge of impending trials, whether of the church or of the world's plagues—he who is called the Advocate, that is, the advocate for entreating the judge—commanded remedies of this kind of service, for example, now for practicing the discipline of sobriety and self-control. We who receive him necessarily also observe what he then established. Look at the Jewish fasts and you will find nothing new, if all later generations guard by hereditary religion what was commanded to the fathers. Moreover, throughout Greece those councils are held in certain places from all the churches, through which even the deeper matters are handled in common, and the very representation of the whole Christian name is celebrated with great veneration. And how worthy of the faith that inaugurates it, to gather from everywhere to Christ! See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity (Psalm 133:1)! You do not readily know how to sing this, except at the time when you dine with many others. But those assemblies, having first labored with station fasts and fastings, know how to mourn with those who mourn and only then to rejoice with those who rejoice. If we also in different provinces perform those solemn observances, which the word then present defended, representing one another in the Spirit, it is the law of the sacrament.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that the church's solemn fasts are fixed by Scripture or tradition and that nothing more may be added.

title: New observances for a new condition in Christ
english: So when we observe times and days and months and years, are we behaving like the Galatians? Certainly, if we are observing Jewish ceremonies and legal solemnities. For the apostle unteaches those things. He checks the persistence of the old testament buried in Christ and establishes the new. But if the condition in Christ is new, then new solemnities ought to exist as well. Or if the apostle scraped away every devotion of times and days and months and years entirely, why do we celebrate Passover in an annual cycle in the first month? Why do we run through the fifty days after it in all exultation? Why do we dedicate Wednesday and Friday to station fasts, and the Preparation Day to fastings? Although you also sometimes keep the Sabbath unbroken, you say that one must never fast except at Passover, according to the reasoning given elsewhere. For us, certainly, every day is celebrated even by common consecration. So there is no reasoning of distinction with the apostle, who distinguishes new and old. But here too your inconsistency will be laughed at, when you reproach us with the form of old things in the very matter where you accuse the cause of newness.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that observing times, days, months, and years makes his group guilty of the Galatian error, by arguing that the apostle abolished only Jewish and old-covenant observances, not all devotional times.

title: The apostle's own words condemn the critics of fasting
english: He also reproves those who would command people to abstain from foods—but on the basis of the Holy Spirit's providence, condemning in advance the heretics who would prescribe perpetual abstinence in order to destroy and despise the Creator's works. Such people I find among Marcion, among Tatian, among Ioues, that modern heretic derived from Pythagoras—but not among the Advocate. For how small is our restriction of foods? We offer to God two weeks of dry-food fasts in the year, and not even complete weeks, excluding of course the Sabbaths and Lord's days, abstaining from things we do not reject but merely postpone. And yet, writing to the Romans, he now stings you as detractors of this duty. "Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food," he says (Romans 14:20). What work? The one about which he says: "It is good not to eat meat or drink wine" (Romans 14:21). For the one who serves in these matters is pleasing and acceptable to our God. "One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables; let the one who eats not nullify the one who does not eat" (Romans 14:2-3). "Who are you to judge another man's servant?" (Romans 14:4). "Both the one who eats and the one who does not eat gives thanks to God" (Romans 14:6). But when he forbids controversy to arise by human judgment, how much more by divine judgment? So he knew that some accuse those who discipline and restrict their diet—people who abstain from disdain, not from duty—but approve those who do so in honor of the Creator, not in insult to him. And if he handed you the keys of the meat market, permitting everything to be eaten in order to establish the exception for idol-sacrificed things, he did not therefore shut up the kingdom of God in the meat market. For he says, "The kingdom of God is not eating and drinking" (Romans 14:17), and "Food does not commend us to God" (1 Corinthians 8:8)—not so that you should think this was said about dry food, but rather about rich and elaborate food. Indeed, when he adds, "If we eat, we are no better off, and if we do not eat, we are no worse off" (1 Corinthians 8:8), he thunders more at you, who think you are better off if you eat and worse off if you do not, and that is why you disparage these practices. How unworthily you also interpret the Lord to suit your own appetite, as one who ate and drank indiscriminately. But I think that he also fasted—he who pronounced blessed not those who are full, but those who hunger and thirst (Matthew 5:6); he who declared his food to be not what the disciples supposed, but the completion of the Father's work (John 4:34), teaching them to work for the food that endures to eternal life (John 6:27); who in the ordinary prayer commanded us to ask for bread (Matthew 6:11), not for Attalic riches. So too Isaiah did not deny that God had chosen fasting, but he listed what kind of fasting God had not chosen. "In the days of your fasts," he says, "your own desires are found, and you oppress all who are subject to you; you fast for quarrels and strife and strike with the fist. I did not choose such a fast" (Isaiah 58:3-5)—but the kind he went on to describe, and by describing it he did not take away fasting but confirmed it.
orientation: Tertullian is answering opponents who cite Paul against food restrictions, and he now turns Paul's words back on them.

title: Fasting vindicated by Israel's examples and pagan imitation
english: For even if he prefers works of justice, he does not prefer them without sacrifice: the sacrifice of a soul afflicted by fasts. Certainly the God who was not pleased by a people lacking self-control in gluttony was not pleased by such a priest or prophet either.  (A closer alternative: "Surely this is the God whom no people, no priest and no prophet lacking self-control in gluttony pleased.") The monuments of desire still stand where the people most greedy for flesh were buried, belching out quail-meat all the way to cholera. The elder Eli is dashed down before the temple doors, his sons fall in the battle line, his daughter-in-law breathes her last in childbirth. This was the blow the shameless house deserved from God, for it cheated the fleshly sacrifices.

Shemaiah, a man of God, had prophesied the end of the idolatry introduced by King Jeroboam. After the king's hand withered and was immediately restored, after the altar split apart, the king invited him to make amends because of these signs. But Shemaiah plainly excused himself from touching any food there at all, for God had forbidden him. Soon afterward, however, another old man lied about being a prophet and fed him recklessly. According to the word of God spoken there at the table, Shemaiah was not buried among his fathers. Struck down by a lion's attack on the road and buried among strangers, he paid the penalty of the fast he had abandoned.

These will be examples both to the people and to bishops, even spiritual ones, if they admit any lack of self-control in gluttony. But the warning did not cease even among the dead. There the rich man's feasts are tormented, while the poor man's fasts are refreshed, and they have Moses and the prophets as teachers. For Joel also cried out: "Sanctify a fast and proclaim a service" (Joel 2:15, LXX), foreseeing even then that other apostles and prophets would sanctify fasting and proclaim services that care for God. This is why those who fawn over idols by dressing them and adorning them and greeting them at every hour are said to offer service.

But the nations also recognize every kind of self-humbling. When the sky is stunned and the year is parched, barefoot processions are announced, magistrates lay aside their purple, they turn the fasces backward, they call for prayer, they renew sacrifice. In certain colonies, moreover, by an annual rite they cover themselves with sackcloth and sprinkle themselves with ashes and offer fasting as a suppliant to their idols. Baths and shops are closed until the ninth hour. There is one public fire at the altars, and no water even in the dishes. A Ninevite cessation of work, I believe. Certainly a Jewish fast is celebrated everywhere, when temples are abandoned and along every shore, wherever in the open air, they now send prayer to heaven. And although they disgrace the gift of mourning with their worship and adornment, still they strive for the faith of abstinence and sigh for the authority of the star that delays.

But it is well that you, hurling blasphemies at our dry-food fasts, equate them with the abstinence rites of Isis and Cybele. I accept the comparison as testimony. From this it will be established that the practice is divine, since the devil, the imitator of divine things, copies it. From truth falsehood is built; from religion superstition is put together. This is why you are the more irreligious, the more ready the pagan is. He, after all, slaughters his gluttony to an idol; you do not want to do so to God. For your god is your belly, and your lung is the temple, and your paunch is the altar, and the cook is the priest, and the holy spirit is the aroma, and the seasonings are spiritual gifts, and the belching is prophecy.
orientation: Tertullian is answering opponents who cite Isaiah 58 to claim God prefers works of justice over fasting, and he now piles up Old Testament examples showing that neglecting fasting brought punishment, then turns to pagan practices that imitate fasting.

title: Gluttony versus the lean body of faith
english: You are old, if we want to speak the truth: you who indulge so much in gluttony, and rightly you boast that you are first. I always recognize the taste of Esau the hunter of wild beasts in you. So you devote yourself everywhere to tracking down thrushes, so you come in from the field of your utterly undisciplined way of life, so you grow faint in spirit. If I offer you lentil stew reddened with reduced wine, you will immediately sell all your birthrights.

Among you the love-feast boils in pots, faith is warmed at the hearth, hope is spread out on serving dishes. But the love-feast is the greater thing, because through it your young men sleep with the sisters. These are, of course, the appendages of gluttony: wantonness and luxuries. The apostle knew this association when, after first saying not in drunkenness nor in revelings, he added nor in beds and lusts (Romans 13:13). It belongs to the indictment of your gluttony that among you a double honor for those who preside is assigned in double portions of food, when the apostle gave double honor to both brothers and leaders (1 Timothy 5:17). Who is holier among you than the one who feasts more often, who provides more lavish banquets, who is better equipped with drinking cups?

Rightly do you who are people of soul and flesh alone reject spiritual things. If the prophets pleased such people, they would not be mine. Why then do you not openly proclaim: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (1 Corinthians 15:32)? Just as we do not hesitate to command openly: Let us fast, brothers and sisters, lest perhaps tomorrow we die. Let us openly defend our disciplines.

We are certain that those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Romans 8:8)—not, of course, in the substance of the flesh, but in its care, in its affection, in its activity, in its will. Leanness does not displease us. For God did not give the flesh by weight, just as he did not give the Spirit by measure. More easily, perhaps, will the thinner flesh enter through the narrow gate of salvation (Matthew 7:13-14); more quickly will the lighter flesh be raised; longer will the drier flesh endure in the tomb.

Let the boxers and Olympic wrestlers be fattened. Ambition of the body suits those who also need strength—and yet even they grow strong on dry-food fasts. But our strengths are different, and our powers are different, just as our contests are different. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the powers of the world, against spiritual forces of wickedness (Ephesians 6:12). Against these one must stand not with flesh and blood, but with faith and a strong spirit. Besides, a fatter Christian will perhaps be more useful to bears and lions than to God—except that even against wild beasts he will need to practice leanness.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing an unspiritual Christian opponent directly, contrasting his gluttonous lifestyle with the fasting discipline he defends.
